cards.front: What defines a 3D shape as a prism?
cards.back: It has the same 2D shape (cross-section) repeated throughout its length.

options.text: It has the same 2D shape (cross-section) repeated throughout its length.
options.explanation: A prism has a constant cross-section along its entire length, so every slice perpendicular to that length has the same shape and dimensions.

options.text: It has the same 2D shape (cross-section) at each end only.
options.explanation: Having identical shapes only at the two ends does not guarantee a prism, because the shape could change between them. The cross-section must remain the same throughout its length.

options.text: It has a changing 2D shape (cross-section) throughout its length.
options.explanation: This describes a solid whose cross-section changes along its length, such as a pyramid. In a prism, the same cross-section is repeated throughout the entire length.

options.text: It has the same volume in every direction throughout its length.
options.explanation: A constant volume does not define a type of three-dimensional shape. A prism is defined by having the same two-dimensional cross-section throughout its length.

cards.front: The volume of any prism is calculated using the formula: $V = \text{[...]} \times \text{length}$.
cards.back: The volume of any prism is calculated using the formula: $V = \boxed{\text{area of cross-section}} \times \text{length}$.

options.explanation: A prism is formed by extending a constant cross-section through a length, so its volume equals the cross-sectional area multiplied by that length.
Perimeter measures the distance around the cross-section rather than the space inside it. Volume requires the area of the cross-section multiplied by the prism’s length.
The area of a prism’s surface is not used directly to calculate its volume. The required factor is the area of its constant cross-section.
Using the cross-sectional width alone omits another dimension and produces square rather than cubic units. The area of the cross-section must be multiplied by the length.

cards.front: The volume of any prism is calculated using the formula: $V = \text{area of cross-section} \times \text{[...]}$.
cards.back: The volume of any prism is calculated using the formula: $V = \text{area of cross-section} \times \boxed{\text{length}}$.

options.explanation: Multiplying the cross-sectional area by the distance through which that cross-section extends gives the prism’s volume in cubic units.
The perimeter describes the boundary of the cross-section and is not the distance through which it extends. The required multiplier is the prism’s length.
Width may be one dimension within the cross-section, so multiplying by it can count a cross-sectional dimension twice. The correct multiplier is the prism’s length.
Height may be needed when finding the cross-sectional area, but it is not necessarily the extrusion distance. The area must be multiplied by the prism’s length.

cards.front: What does the length of a prism represent in the volume formula?
cards.back: The direction the cross-section has been stretched.

options.text: The direction the cross-section has been stretched.
options.explanation: The length is the extrusion distance: it measures how far the unchanged cross-section continues through the prism, perpendicular to the cross-sectional face.

options.text: The distance around the edge of the cross-section.
options.explanation: The distance around the cross-section is its perimeter, not the prism’s length. Length measures the direction in which the cross-section has been stretched.

options.text: The distance across the height of the cross-section.
options.explanation: The perpendicular height may be used to calculate the cross-sectional area. The prism’s length instead measures the direction through which that cross-section extends.

options.text: The direction of the longest edge of the prism.
options.explanation: The longest edge is not automatically the length used in the prism formula. The relevant length is the direction in which the cross-section has been stretched.

cards.front: What is the formula for the volume of a cuboid?
cards.back: $$V = \text{length} \times \text{width} \times \text{height}$

options.explanation: A cuboid has a rectangular cross-section, so multiplying its area, length times width, by its height gives the product of all three perpendicular dimensions.
Adding the three dimensions does not calculate three-dimensional space and does not produce cubic units. A cuboid’s volume is their product: length times width times height.
This multiplies only two dimensions, so it gives the area of a rectangular face rather than volume. The height must also be included.
The factor of one half belongs to triangular prisms, not cuboids. A cuboid’s rectangular cross-section requires the full product of length, width and height.

cards.front: When calculating a triangular cross-section, which side length must be avoided for height?
cards.back: The sloping side (unless it is perpendicular to the base).

options.text: The sloping side (unless it is perpendicular to the base).
options.explanation: A triangle’s height must meet the chosen base at a right angle. A sloping side can be used only when it is perpendicular to that base.

options.text: The perpendicular side (even when it forms a right angle).
options.explanation: The perpendicular side is exactly the measurement needed as the triangle’s height. The side to avoid is a sloping side unless it meets the base at a right angle.

options.text: The horizontal base (unless it is the longest side).
options.explanation: The base is required in the triangle area formula and is not automatically the height. The measurement to avoid as height is a non-perpendicular sloping side.

options.text: The vertical side (even when it is perpendicular to the base).
options.explanation: A vertical line can serve as the height when it is perpendicular to the selected base. The unreliable choice is a sloping side that is not perpendicular.

cards.front: State the formula for the area of a trapezium cross-section.
cards.back: $$A = \frac{1}{2}(a+b)h$, where $a, b$ are parallel sides$h$ is perpendicular height

options.text: $$A = \frac{1}{2}(a+b)h$, where $a, b$ are parallel sides$h$ is perpendicular height
options.explanation: A trapezium’s area is the mean of its two parallel side lengths multiplied by their perpendicular separation, giving $\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h$.

options.text: $$A = (a+b)h$, where $a, b$ are parallel sides$h$ is perpendicular height
options.explanation: Omitting the factor of one half doubles the trapezium’s area. The correct formula averages the parallel sides before multiplying by the perpendicular height.

options.text: $$A = \frac{1}{2}(a-b)h$, where $a, b$ are parallel sides$h$ is perpendicular height
options.explanation: Subtracting the parallel sides finds their difference rather than their mean and does not give the trapezium’s area. Their lengths must be added, halved and multiplied by height.

options.text: $$A = \frac{1}{2}(ab)h$, where $a, b$ are parallel sides$h$ is perpendicular height
options.explanation: Multiplying the two parallel sides together is not part of the trapezium formula and gives incorrect dimensions after multiplying by height. Their sum must be halved instead.

cards.front: For unit conversions: $1\text{ m} = \text{[...]}\text{ cm}$ and $1\text{ litre} = 1000\text{ cm}^3$.
cards.back: For unit conversions: $1\text{ m} = \boxed{100}\text{ cm}$ and $1\text{ litre} = 1000\text{ cm}^3$.

options.explanation: The prefix centi- means one hundredth of a metre, so one metre contains 100 centimetres. This is a linear conversion, not a cubic conversion.
This confuses centimetres with a ten-part conversion. Since each centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, one metre equals 100 centimetres.
This copies the litre-to-cubic-centimetre conversion into a linear length conversion. One metre contains 100 centimetres, whereas one litre contains 1000 cubic centimetres.
This reverses the conversion and treats metres per centimetre as centimetres per metre. One centimetre is 0.01 metres, but one metre is 100 centimetres.

cards.front: For unit conversions: $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$ and $1\text{ litre} = \text{[...]}\text{ cm}^3$.
cards.back: For unit conversions: $1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$ and $1\text{ litre} = \boxed{1000}\text{ cm}^3$.

options.explanation: One litre occupies exactly $1000\text{ cm}^3$, because one millilitre equals $1\text{ cm}^3$ and there are $1000$ millilitres in a litre.
This incorrectly applies the linear conversion $1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}$ to volume. One litre contains $1000$ millilitres, so it equals $1000\text{ cm}^3$.
This results from adding an extra factor of ten during conversion. Since $1\text{ ml}=1\text{ cm}^3$ and $1\text{ litre}=1000\text{ ml}$, the correct value is $1000$.
This confuses a litre with a cubic metre: $1\text{ m}^3=1\,000\,000\text{ cm}^3$. A litre is much smaller and equals $1000\text{ cm}^3$.

cards.front: How do you find the volume of a prism with a composite (e.g. L-shaped) cross-section?
cards.back: Split cross-section into simpler shapes (rectangles/triangles)Sum the individual areasMultiply total area by prism length

options.text: Split cross-section into simpler shapes (rectangles/triangles)Sum the individual areasMultiply total area by prism length
options.explanation: A composite cross-section can be divided into familiar shapes whose areas are added. Multiplying this total cross-sectional area by the constant prism length gives the volume.

options.text: Split cross-section into simpler shapes (rectangles/triangles)Sum the individual perimetersMultiply total perimeter by prism length
options.explanation: Using perimeter gives the lateral surface area rather than volume. The individual cross-sectional areas must be added, then multiplied by the prism length.

options.text: Split cross-section into simpler shapes (rectangles/triangles)Sum the individual areasDivide total area by prism length
options.explanation: Dividing area by length does not produce cubic units. Volume is found by multiplying the total cross-sectional area by the prism length.

options.text: Split cross-section into simpler shapes (rectangles/triangles)Multiply the individual areasMultiply total area by prism length
options.explanation: The areas of separate parts must be added because together they form the whole cross-section. Multiplying those areas together has no geometric meaning for this volume calculation.

cards.front: If the volume and two dimensions of a cuboid are known, how is the missing dimension found?
cards.back: Multiply the known dimensionsDivide the volume by that product

options.text: Multiply the known dimensionsDivide the volume by that product
options.explanation: For a cuboid, $V=lwh$. Multiplying the two known dimensions gives their product, and dividing the volume by it isolates the missing dimension.

options.text: Add the known dimensionsDivide the volume by that total
options.explanation: The cuboid volume formula multiplies dimensions rather than adding them. Multiply the two known dimensions, then divide the volume by their product to find the missing dimension.

options.text: Multiply the known dimensionsMultiply the volume by that product
options.explanation: Multiplying again makes the units and value too large. Since the known dimensions are factors of the volume, divide the volume by their product.

options.text: Divide the known dimensionsMultiply the volume by that quotient
options.explanation: Dividing the known dimensions does not rearrange $V=lwh$ correctly. Their product must divide the volume, leaving the missing dimension in linear units.

cards.front: Capacity is the amount of $\text{[...]}$ a container can hold, often measured in $litres$ or millilitres.
cards.back: Capacity is the amount of $\boxed{liquid}$ a container can hold, often measured in $litres$ or millilitres.

options.explanation: Capacity describes how much liquid a container can hold. It is commonly measured in litres or millilitres, which are units used for liquid volume.
Mass measures the quantity of matter and is usually measured in grams or kilograms. Capacity instead describes the amount of liquid a container can hold.
Surface refers to an outer boundary and would be measured using area units. Capacity concerns the amount of liquid held inside a container.
Length is a one-dimensional measurement recorded in units such as centimetres or metres. Capacity measures the amount of liquid a container can hold.

cards.front: Capacity is the amount of $liquid$ a container can hold, often measured in $\text{[...]}$ or millilitres.
cards.back: Capacity is the amount of $liquid$ a container can hold, often measured in $\boxed{litres}$ or millilitres.

options.explanation: Litres and millilitres are standard metric units of capacity. One litre equals $1000$ millilitres, so both units measure how much liquid a container can hold.
Metres measure length, not capacity. Capacity is commonly measured in litres or millilitres because these units describe the volume of liquid held.
Grams measure mass rather than capacity. The amount of liquid a container can hold is measured in litres or millilitres.
Hectares measure large areas of land, not the volume of a container. Capacity is measured in litres or millilitres.

cards.front: How do you find the side length of a cube if you only know the area of one face?
cards.back: Calculate the square root of the face area.

options.text: Calculate the square root of the face area.
options.explanation: Each face of a cube is a square with area $s^2$. Taking the square root of the face area therefore gives the side length $s$.

options.text: Calculate the cube root of the face area.
options.explanation: A cube root is used to recover a side length from a cube's volume, not from a face area. Since face area is $s^2$, use the square root.

options.text: Calculate the square of the face area.
options.explanation: Squaring the face area increases the power and cannot produce a length. The face area equals $s^2$, so take its square root to obtain $s$.

options.text: Calculate the quarter of the face area.
options.explanation: Dividing by four would relate a square's perimeter to its side, not its area. For face area $s^2$, the side length is its square root.

cards.front: Outline the steps to find a cube's volume from its total surface area.
cards.back: Divide surface area by 6 to get one face areaFind the square root to get side lengthCube the side length ($s^3$)

options.text: Divide surface area by 6 to get one face areaFind the square root to get side lengthCube the side length ($s^3$)
options.explanation: A cube has six identical square faces, so dividing by six gives $s^2$. Its square root gives $s$, and cubing $s$ gives the volume.

options.text: Divide surface area by 4 to get one face areaFind the square root to get side lengthCube the side length ($s^3$)
options.explanation: Dividing by four counts only the lateral faces and ignores the top and bottom. A cube has six equal faces, so first divide the surface area by six.

options.text: Divide surface area by 6 to get one face areaFind the cube root to get side lengthCube the side length ($s^3$)
options.explanation: One face has area $s^2$, so its side is found using a square root, not a cube root. The resulting side length is then cubed.

options.text: Divide surface area by 6 to get one face areaFind the square root to get side lengthSquare the side length ($s^2$)
options.explanation: Squaring the side length returns the area of one face rather than the cube's volume. Volume requires three dimensions, so the side length must be cubed.

cards.front: The relationship between millilitres and cubic centimetres is: $1\text{ ml} = \text{[...]}$.
cards.back: The relationship between millilitres and cubic centimetres is: $1\text{ ml} = \boxed{1\text{ cm}^3}$.

options.explanation: A millilitre is defined as the same volume as one cubic centimetre. Therefore, $1\text{ ml}=1\text{ cm}^3$ exactly.
This introduces an unnecessary factor of ten. Millilitres and cubic centimetres correspond directly, so $1\text{ ml}$ equals exactly $1\text{ cm}^3$.
This confuses the centimetre conversion for length with a capacity conversion. One millilitre occupies only $1\text{ cm}^3$, not $100\text{ cm}^3$.
This is the cubic-centimetre equivalent of one litre, not one millilitre. Since a litre contains $1000$ millilitres, each millilitre equals $1\text{ cm}^3$.

cards.front: Why might a volume comparison not perfectly predict how many boxes fit in a van?
cards.back: Boxes must fit along specific dimensions (length, width, height) without awkward gaps.

options.text: Boxes must fit along specific dimensions (length, width, height) without awkward gaps.
options.explanation: Equal or suitable total volumes do not guarantee a practical arrangement. Each box must fit within the van’s individual dimensions, and unused gaps may remain.

options.text: Boxes only need to have a smaller total volume than the van, regardless of their dimensions.
options.explanation: Comparing total volumes alone ignores the arrangement of the boxes. The correct explanation is that boxes must fit along specific dimensions without leaving awkward gaps.

options.text: Boxes can always be fitted by changing their dimensions while keeping their volume constant.
options.explanation: This assumes rigid boxes can be reshaped, which is not normally possible. Boxes must fit along the van’s specific length, width and height without awkward gaps.

options.text: Boxes will fill the van exactly if their combined volume equals the van’s volume.
options.explanation: Equal combined volume does not ensure that the boxes tessellate inside the available space. Their specific dimensions may prevent them fitting without awkward gaps.

cards.front: Volume is measured in $\text{[...]}$ units, such as $cm^3$, whereas area is measured in $square$ units, such as $cm^2$.
cards.back: Volume is measured in $\boxed{cubic}$ units, such as $cm^3$, whereas area is measured in $square$ units, such as $cm^2$.

options.explanation: Volume measures three-dimensional space, so its units are cubic. For example, multiplying centimetres in three dimensions produces cubic centimetres, written $cm^3$.
Square units measure two-dimensional area, not three-dimensional volume. Volume is measured in cubic units because three lengths are multiplied together.
Linear units measure one-dimensional length rather than volume. The correct term is cubic because volume involves three dimensions and uses units such as $cm^3$.
Decimal describes a way of writing numbers, not the dimension of a unit. Volume is measured in cubic units, such as $cm^3$.

cards.front: Volume is measured in $cubic$ units, such as $cm^3$, whereas area is measured in $\text{[...]}$ units, such as $cm^2$.
cards.back: Volume is measured in $cubic$ units, such as $cm^3$, whereas area is measured in $\boxed{square}$ units, such as $cm^2$.

options.explanation: Area measures a two-dimensional surface, so its units are square units. Multiplying two lengths measured in centimetres gives square centimetres, written $cm^2$.
Cubic units measure three-dimensional volume rather than area. Area involves two dimensions, so it is measured in square units such as $cm^2$.
Linear units measure one-dimensional length rather than two-dimensional area. The correct term is square because area is found by multiplying two lengths.
Decimal refers to number notation and does not describe area units. Area is measured in square units because it covers two dimensions.

cards.front: How do you convert litres to cm³?
cards.back: Multiply by 1000.

options.explanation: One litre equals $1000\text{ cm}^3$, so multiplying the number of litres by $1000$ gives the corresponding volume in cubic centimetres.
Dividing by $1000$ converts cubic centimetres to litres, so this reverses the required conversion. To convert litres to $cm^3$, multiply by $1000$.
This confuses a volume conversion with a smaller scale factor. One litre contains $1000\text{ cm}^3$, so the number of litres must be multiplied by $1000$.
This uses both the wrong operation and the wrong conversion factor. Since $1$ litre equals $1000\text{ cm}^3$, multiply by $1000$.

cards.front: A cube has a square face with area $36\text{ cm}^2$. What is its volume?
cards.back: $$216\text{ cm}^3$ (Side is $6$, and $6 \times 6 \times 6 = 216$).

options.explanation: The square face has side length $\sqrt{36}=6$ cm. Cubing this side length gives the cube’s volume: $6^3=216\text{ cm}^3$.

options.text: $$36\text{ cm}^3$ (The face area is used directly as the volume).
options.explanation: This confuses the two-dimensional face area with the three-dimensional volume. The side is $\sqrt{36}=6$ cm, so the volume is $6^3=216\text{ cm}^3$.
This treats the face area as a side length and then squares it. The actual side is $\sqrt{36}=6$ cm, giving volume $6^3=216\text{ cm}^3$.
This adds the three dimensions instead of multiplying them. A cube’s volume is length times width times height, so $6\times6\times6=216\text{ cm}^3$.
